content.comment_body: Hello everyone, I observed that the default Modbus mapping on [product_name] allows a Modbus master to directly write to any I/O of the base module. Is there a way to restrict this? I want to prevent end users from directly controlling the module's I/O.

Is your [product_name] set as a slave? If so, isn't this standard behavior? Or is it in master mode? From my understanding, when in master mode you can't change any outputs modified by your program or simulate input changes; you can only read the current I/O status and modify the VM.

Hello, if someone is familiar with [product_name] and Modbus, they can set it up accordingly. If you want to stop others from editing the program on [product_name], make use of the password protection features. By default, Modbus isn't active on a new module—you have to configure the connection and specifically define which data (DI, coils, or registers) should be exchanged. Hope this helps.

My aim is to prevent accidental or unauthorized changes to the circuit connected via Modbus. I want to block access to any registers that I haven't intentionally enabled, because otherwise an external device could directly change the I/O, which is a problem.

As I mentioned before, in my tests, outputs shown in the program diagram are set as read-only by [product_name], and similarly any parameters tied to VM addresses become read-only. You might want to confirm whether outputs can be changed from your side. Inputs are mapped to Input Status (not Coils), making them read-only by design.

I ran experiments and noticed that when a digital output is tied to a program block, external writes from a Modbus master don't alter it. It seems that [product_name] gives priority to its internal logic over external commands. Earlier, I hadn't used these I/O points in my program and thought that an external Modbus write could change them. Thanks for the clarification!

analysis.insight_summary: Forum members are focused on protecting the security and functionality of their [product_name] base modules when integrating Modbus communication. There's a concern that default Modbus settings might permit outside devices to directly modify I/O registers. The discussion clarifies some misunderstandings about Modbus permissions and highlights that proper programming and configuration can limit external control over critical I/O functions.
analysis.user_expectations: Users want an easy and safe method to restrict Modbus master write access exclusively to chosen and pre-configured registers, making sure unauthorized devices cannot manipulate vital I/O elements.
